problems.title: Sizing a grid
problems.statement: A kernel processes $n = 1{,}000{,}000$ elements, one per thread, with blocks of 256 threads.

parts.prompt: Threads that must do nothing (fail the bounds check)?

problems.solution: (a) $\lceil 10^6/256 \rceil = 3907$. (b) $3907 \times 256 - 10^6 = 192$. Without the if (i < n) guard those 192 threads would read and write past the end of the arrays: on a real GPU that's silent memory corruption or a crash.

problems.title: Who am I?
problems.statement: In a 1-D launch with blockDim.x = 128, consider the thread with blockIdx.x = 5, threadIdx.x = 37.

parts.prompt: Which warp of its block is it in (0-based)?

hints: Warps are consecutive groups of 32 threads within a block.
problems.solution: (a) $5 \times 128 + 37 = 677$. (b) $\lfloor 37/32 \rfloor = 1$. (c) $37 \bmod 32 = 5$. Warps are formed from consecutive threadIdx values within a block, which is why the layout of threads over data decides what a warp's 32 lanes touch together (Parts 1 and 2).

problems.title: A 2-D launch over an image
problems.statement: A 1920 × 1080 image, one thread per pixel, with 16 × 16 blocks. x = blockIdx.x·16 + threadIdx.x indexes columns.
problems.solution: (a) $1920/16 = 120$. (b) $\lceil 1080/16 \rceil = 68$ (67.5). (c) $120 \times 68 \times 256 = 2{,}088{,}960$. (d) $2{,}088{,}960 - 1920 \times 1080 = 15{,}360$: the last row of blocks is half outside the image. In 2-D, guard both coordinates: if (x < W && y < H).

problems.title: Waves and the tail
problems.statement: 1,000 equal blocks run on a GPU with 34 SMs, each holding 4 of these blocks at a time.

parts.prompt: Fraction of the machine busy in the last wave, in %?

problems.solution: Slots $= 34 \times 4 = 136$. (a) $\lceil 1000/136 \rceil = 8$. (b) $1000 - 7 \times 136 = 48$. (c) $48/136 = 35.3\%$. (d) $1000/(8 \times 136) = 91.9\%$. With 1,088 blocks you'd do 8.8% more work in the same time. Part 5 turns this into a design tool.

problems.title: What limits residency?
problems.statement: An SM allows at most 2,048 threads, 32 blocks and 65,536 registers. A kernel uses blocks of 128 threads and 64 registers per thread.

parts.prompt: Blocks allowed by the thread limit?
Blocks allowed by the register limit?

hints: Compute each limit separately; the smallest wins.
problems.solution: (a) $2048/128 = 16$. (b) Registers per block $= 128 \times 64 = 8192$, so $65536/8192 = 8$. (c) $\min(16, 32, 8) = 8$ blocks = 1,024 threads, 50% occupancy. (d) Registers. Part 2 builds the full calculator, including shared memory and allocation granularity.

problems.title: Grid-stride loops
problems.statement: Instead of one thread per element, you launch a fixed 136 blocks × 256 threads and loop: for (i = global id; i < n; i += total threads), with $n = 10^7$.

parts.prompt: How many threads do that many?

hints: n = q × threads + r: r threads do q + 1 iterations.
problems.solution: (a) $136 \times 256 = 34{,}816$. (b) $\lceil 10^7/34816 \rceil = 288$. (c) $10^7 - 287 \times 34816 = 7{,}808$ threads do 288; the rest do 287. Grid-stride loops decouple the grid size from the problem size, so you can size the grid to the machine (a whole number of waves) and reuse per-thread setup across many elements.

problems.title: Counting a GPU's concurrency
problems.statement: A GPU has 108 SMs, each holding up to 2,048 resident threads.

parts.prompt: Bytes in flight if each has one 4-byte load outstanding?

problems.solution: (a) $108 \times 2048 = 221{,}184$. (b) $\times 4 = 884{,}736$ bytes: the same order as Little's law demands for a ~2 TB/s, ~500 ns memory. The design follows from the constraint.

problems.title: Your RTX 2060 Super
problems.statement: The RTX 2060 Super (Turing) has 34 SMs, at most 32 resident warps per SM, and 448 GB/s of memory bandwidth. Assume 450 ns loaded latency, and a streaming kernel where each warp load moves 128 bytes.

parts.prompt: Bytes in flight needed for full bandwidth?
Bytes in flight with every warp resident and one load each?
Best achievable fraction of peak with one load per warp, in %?
Minimum independent loads per warp to saturate?

hints: Turing allows half as many resident warps per SM as the 64 of newer datacenter GPUs.
problems.solution: (a) $448 \times 450 = 201{,}600$ bytes. (b) $34 \times 32 \times 128 = 139{,}264$. (c) $69.1\%$. (d) $\lceil 201600/139264 \rceil = 2$. On your card, a simple one-element-per-thread copy kernel can't reach peak bandwidth even at full occupancy: you'll see this when you measure it on real hardware, and fix it by having each thread load 2–4 elements (or use 128-bit vector loads) before storing.

problems.title: Odd block sizes
hints: Warps are always 32 lanes; a partial warp still occupies a whole one.
problems.solution: (a) $\lceil 100/32 \rceil = 4$. (b) $128 - 100 = 28$. (c) $100/128 = 78.1\%$. Block sizes should be multiples of 32 (usually of 64 or 128): the hardware schedules whole warps.

problems.title: Choosing a block size
problems.statement: An SM allows 2,048 threads and 16 blocks; registers and shared memory aren't limiting.

parts.prompt: Occupancy with blocks of 64 threads, in %?

problems.solution: (a) $\min(16, 32) = 16$ blocks × 64 = 1024 threads: 50%. (b) $\min(16, 21) = 16$ × 96 = 1536: 75%. (c) $\min(16, 16) = 16$ × 128 = 2048: 100%. (d) 2 × 1024 = 2048: 100%. Small blocks hit the per-SM block limit before the thread limit. Very large blocks reach full occupancy but are coarse: one block that can't fit wastes a lot, and the tail effect grows.
